logline: A Pakistani-American college student wakes up next to a murdered woman after a blackout night in Manhattan, and is drawn into a legal machinery that transforms him long before the verdict is read.

renewal.note: The Night Of was a standalone eight-episode limited series adapted from the BBC drama Criminal Justice. No sequel or continuation has been produced.

bollymeter.basis: A 94% Rotten Tomatoes score, a Metacritic score of 90 from 40 critics, and an 8.4 IMDb rating place it among HBO's most critically praised limited series; Riz Ahmed's performance is the consistent anchor of that consensus.

pull_quotes.text: Compulsively watchable and extraordinarily rewarding, a brilliant and addictive mystery.
The Night Of is a richly crafted, exquisitely performed mystery that will keep viewers enthralled.

seasons.review_body: Airing on HBO from July to August 2016, The Night Of arrived as the definitive successor to the literary crime drama tradition Richard Price and Steve Zaillian had each built separately. Critics rated it 94% on Rotten Tomatoes from 88 reviews and awarded it a Metacritic score of 90, with Variety calling it compulsively watchable and Ebert's site positioning it as an essential American legal portrait. The show earned 14 Emmy nominations and won five, including Outstanding Lead Actor for Riz Ahmed. The consensus fixed on two achievements: the show's refusal to function as a simple whodunit and its unflinching portrait of what incarceration does to a person before any verdict is delivered. The audience at 8.4 on IMDb registered the same conviction.

episode_reviews.title: The Beach
episode_reviews.review_body: The Night Of Season 1 Episode 1 'The Beach' aired July 10, 2016 on HBO as the series premiere. Rotten Tomatoes holds Season 1 at 94 percent from 88 critics; Metacritic scored it 90. Variety called it 'compulsively watchable and extraordinarily rewarding, a brilliant and addictive mystery.' The premiere follows a single night in real time across borrowed cab, wrong fare, and a party that ends in catastrophe - Richard Price and Steve Zaillian's script accumulates mundane bad decisions with near-Hitchcockian precision, each choice individually explicable and collectively devastating. Riz Ahmed's Naz Khan is introduced as a study in credible ordinariness: a good student, an anxious kid, someone who wants to fit in. The detailing of the Manhattan criminal processing system in the episode's second half is documentary-precise. The final image of Episode 1 is among the most unnerving season-opener endings in HBO history.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere follows a single night in real time as Naz Khan borrows his father's cab, picks up a fare, and ends up in a situation that will define the rest of the series. The filmmaking is almost Hitchcockian in how it accumulates mundane bad decisions into catastrophe, and the final image of the first episode is among the most unnerving season-opener endings in HBO history.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Naz waking in the kitchen of a stranger's apartment - the single frame that crystallises everything the show is about.

episode_reviews.title: The Call of the Wild
episode_reviews.review_body: The Night Of Season 1 Episode 8 'The Call of the Wild' aired August 28, 2016 on HBO as the series finale. Rotten Tomatoes holds Season 1 at 94 percent from 88 critics; the season earned 14 Emmy nominations and 5 wins, including Outstanding Lead Actor for Riz Ahmed. RogerEbert.com called the series 'a richly crafted, exquisitely performed mystery.' The finale delivers a verdict and then refuses the catharsis the genre conventionally provides - what lingers is not the legal outcome but the portrait of Naz after the machinery of justice has run its course. The transformation tracked across eight episodes through small courtroom exchanges, cell dynamics, and Naz's body becoming gradually inscribed with the institution, arrives at a conclusion the episode holds without editorialising. John Turturro's Jack Stone, given the show's funniest subplot and its most rueful grace note, lands the finale's most precisely placed emotional beat.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivers a verdict but refuses the catharsis the genre conventionally provides. What lingers is the portrait of Naz after the machinery of justice has run its course, the transformation the show has been tracking in the background of every courtroom scene. The ending lands with deliberate ambivalence, framing it as the shows final and most honest statement.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Naz emerging from Rikers Island - the moment that forces the question of whether any outcome constitutes justice.
